content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to pre-train a language model that can work well on both language generation tasks and language understanding tasks. Specifically, it proposes a method to combine T-5 with Electra. The method is only tested on base-sized models and results show that the pre-trained model can achieve similar or better results on both understanding and generation tasks compared to T-5.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

It is interesting to know that by training T-5’s encoder in the Electra way, T-5’s generation performance can be improved.

Weaknesses:

1. Lack of verification/explanation of most design choices. I didn’t fully get the authors’ arguments regarding equation 6,7 8 and why they absolutely need to be replaced by equation 9, 10 ,11. For example, the label leakage is caused by teacher forcing instead of equation 6. Instead of feeding the ground truth at position k-1 as the decoder output, one can just either feed the [mask] or the generated token. Have you tried that and see the performance?  I also didn’t understand the argument regarding eq 7. I’m lost at “In Eq. (7), the denoising is performed by the decoder, which has to learn to select which positions to denoise first.”  The ‘h’s should maintain a sequential order if properly implemented right? A clearer illustration might be helpful. Do you have experiments results suggesting that Eq (7) leads to worse performance?
2. In-sufficient experiments. Experiments are only on base-sized models. This bothers me because from my own experience, it is not always true that a new method would work well on all model scales if it works on base models. Actually in most cases it is not true. Therefore it would be more convincing if more model scales are tested.
3. Lack of novelty. Following the authors’ narratives from a T-5 viewpoint, one can feel the authors have made quite a lot of modifications on T-5. But if you directly compare the proposed method with the original Electra, the proposed method just adds a decoder on top of the original ELECTRA. So I feel not surprised that the proposed method can get similar results with Electra on understanding tasks. This is not my main concern though.

content.title: Response to Reviewer R8zZ
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. We updated our paper and added a new appendix section, Appendix A.5, to explain the challenge of “ill-formed target” in detail. We also present new results of larger models in the “general response” post. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> Lack of verification/explanation of most design choices. I didn’t fully get the authors’ arguments regarding equation 6,7 8 and why they absolutely need to be replaced by equation 9, 10 ,11. For example, the label leakage is caused by teacher forcing instead of equation 6. Instead of feeding the ground truth at position k-1 as the decoder output, one can just either feed the [mask] or the generated token. Have you tried that and see the performance? I also didn’t understand the argument regarding eq 7. I’m lost at “In Eq. (7), the denoising is performed by the decoder, which has to learn to select which positions to denoise first.” The ‘h’s should maintain a sequential order if properly implemented right? A clearer illustration might be helpful. Do you have experiments results suggesting that Eq (7) leads to worse performance?

**Ill-formed target.** We add Appendix A.5 with an example to show how such an ill-formed target in Section 3.2 will lead to ambiguities in pretraining the encoder-decoder main model. In practice, the pretraining diverges when the ill-formed target is used.

**Label Leakage.** Teacher forcing is indeed a necessary condition that label leakage happens. However, teacher forcing is the standard practice for training Transformer decoders efficiently, used by almost all Transformer decoders (Vaswani et al., 2017). Also, with i.i.d. random masking we introduced in Section 3.3 and Equation (12), there is no label leakage problem even if we are still using teacher forcing. Ablation studies in Table 4 (comparing Metro-T5 with "continuous span mask") also show significant performance gain of applying i.i.d. random masking and addressing the issue of label leakage.

### Weakness 2

> In-sufficient experiments. Experiments are only on base-sized models. This bothers me because from my own experience, it is not always true that a new method would work well on all model scales if it works on base models. Actually in most cases it is not true. Therefore it would be more convincing if more model scales are tested.

We show results of Metro-T5-Large++ (24L, 1024D, 775M parameters). in the table in the "general response" post. **Metro-T5-Large++ outperforms Metro-T5-Base++ and T0-3B, only 1.8 pts below T0-11B with 7% of its parameters** , the SOTA on encoder-decoder prompt learning with the same set of source tasks. This new experimental result shows that Metro-T5 keeps its performance gain on larger scales.

### Weakness 3

> Lack of novelty. Following the authors’ narratives from a T-5 viewpoint, one can feel the authors have made quite a lot of modifications on T-5. But if you directly compare the proposed method with the original Electra, the proposed method just adds a decoder on top of the original ELECTRA. So I feel not surprised that the proposed method can get similar results with Electra on understanding tasks. This is not my main concern though.

Metro-T5 is indeed inspired by ELECTRA, and the design of the encoder part seems similar. However, the corrective language modeling (CLM) objective on the decoder is a novel technical contribution, and we resolve various technical challenges in incorporating model-generated signals into encoder-decoder pretraining.

Regarding empirical contributions, not only does Metro-T5 outperform ELECTRA on the GLUE NLU benchmark, but it is also a unified encoder-decoder model that is capable of NLG and prompting. Metro-T5 is either on par or outperforms the baselines in NLU, NLG, and prompting. Moreover, Metro-T5-Base++ outperforms the T0-3B model on the T0-Eval benchmark with only 8% of its parameters.

**References**

- Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. Attention is all you need. In NeurIPS, 2017.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Proposes a new pre-training objective/process for T5-like encoder-decoder models. It uses a BART-like (Lewis et al) denoising auto-encoder objective where the noise is provided by an auxiliary MLM-model (similar to ELECTRA, Clark et al). The main and auxiliary models are trained together. 

Experimental results are done at the T5-Base size using data similar to BERT and ROBERTA (i.e. not C4). Models are fine-tuned/evaluated on GLUE, SQuAD, CNN/DM and XSum. Prompt-finetuning results are also provided on the T0 Eval benchmark. The results are usually better than a T5 baseline, where the only difference is the pre-training objective.

Pretraining efficiency seems improved in terms of pretraining time on the equivalent hardware compared to T5.

Authors also present a negative result where they used an LM to generate masked out spans for T5 to denoise. They report unstable training and label leakage as reasons it doesn't work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
- Good results compared to the T5-base baseline
- Elegant idea of applying ELECTRA to encoder-decoders
- Compute appears to be competitive.

# Weaknesses
- Authors only provided results at the T5-Base size. Significant compute was employed to train T5-Base, so it's unclear why larger models were not tried (since access to compute does not seem to be an issue). It would also strengthen the paper to show this objective is better at different scales.
- There are no results on SuperGLUE, which would strengthen results as a harder benchmark
- A more natural comparison would be BART instead of T5, since the main difference is generating noise with an auxiliary model. The training data also appears to be closer to BART (i.e. not C4).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Authors keep trying to relate the work to METRO, which is not as well known as BART/ELEKTRA/T5, and this does not seem necessary at all. The pre-training objective is very similar to BART, but instead the noise is provided by an ELECTRA-like auxiliary model. I would strongly recommend re-writing the paper to relate it to ELECTRA+BART instead of relating to METRO. The former are much better known to most readers and the relationship appears stronger as well.
- For Figure 4, does this pretraining time correspond to FLOPs? Is it possible to simply use FLOPs instead or as well? 
- Reproducibility: There are significant missing details on how to train T5 and the auxiliary model "side-by-side". At least some pseudo-code would be helpful. 
  - e.g. How do you deal with sampling step (generating x^noise) from the auxiliary model? Do you take the argmax?
  - Do you stop gradients for encoder-decoder flowing past x^noise?
  - How do you set the lambda hparams in the loss?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting way to generalize ELECTRA to encoder-decoder models and shows good results at the T5-base size. The main issue is it's unclear how well this advantage persists with larger models and whether it is worth the extra complexity of having the throwaway auxiliary model. I also think writing could be improved by relating to BART instead of METRO and T5. BART is more suitable as the objective there is closer and METRO is a very recent and lesser known work.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response to Reviewer d7ab (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. Thank you for pointing out that we presented an “elegant idea of applying ELECTRA to encoder-decoders”. We updated our paper and added more details into the Appendix A.2 according to your suggestions in the “reproducibility” section. We present new results of larger models in the “general response” post. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> Authors only provided results at the T5-Base size. Significant compute was employed to train T5-Base, so it's unclear why larger models were not tried (since access to compute does not seem to be an issue). It would also strengthen the paper to show this objective is better at different scales.

We agree that the empirical observations may vary at different model scales, and we will face different technical challenges when working with models of huge sizes. That said, we still believe research at base-sized (12L, 768D) models is crucial because: (a) base-sized models are still the most used models, as reflected by the downloading frequency on Huggingface; (b) many research explorations have to start with base-sized models, and then the ideas accumulated in these research explorations can be further explored at a larger scale, perhaps by research institutions with the privileged access of large-scale computing infrastructure. There are many interesting ideas discovered at the base size.

That said, to demonstrate the advantage of **METRO-T5 holds at a larger scale** , we train Metro-T5-Large++ (24L, 1024D, 775M parameters) and present results in the table in the "general response" post. As is shown in the table, Metro-T5-Large++ outperforms Metro-T5-Base++ and T0-3B, only 1.8 pts below T0-11B with 7% of its parameters, the SOTA on encoder-decoder prompt learning. This new experimental result shows that Metro-T5 keeps its performance gain on larger scales. We plan to add more empirical results at large sizes in our next version as finetuning Large++ models is quite time-consuming.

### Weakness 2

> There are no results on SuperGLUE, which would strengthen results as a harder benchmark

In the paper, we compare Metro-T5 with baselines on GLUE (8 subtasks), SQuAD, CNN/DailyMail, XSum, and T0-Eval (9 subtasks). Compared with our related works and other top conference NLP papers, **we do experiments on a wider variety of benchmarks**. For example, ELECTRA (Clark et al., 2020) and COCO-LM (Meng et al., 2021) only do experiments on GLUE and SQuAD, while UniLMv2 (Bao et al., 2020) and BART (Lewis et al., 2019) do experiment on GLUE, SQuAD, CNN/DailyMail, and XSum. None of them evaluates their model on SuperGLUE (and the trend of methods evaluated on both GLUE and SuperGLUE often aligns). Moreover, the **T0-Eval** task mixture for prompt-finetuning, which we used to evaluate Metro-T5, **includes five tasks in SuperGLUE**: CB, COPA, RTE, WiC, and WSC. Table 3 includes the performance of Metro-T5 and baselines on these SuperGLUE tasks in a prompt learning setting.

### Weakness 3

> A more natural comparison would be BART instead of T5, since the main difference is generating noise with an auxiliary model. The training data also appears to be closer to BART (i.e. not C4).

C4 is a massive corpus with 800GB of text cleaned from CommonCrawl. Our Base++ setting uses a text corpus with 160GB of text, and it is indeed more similar to the corpus used in RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) and BART (Lewis et al., 2019). According to the author of T5/C4 (Raffel et al., 2019), a larger corpus usually leads to better performance. So we consider it **fair to compare our Base++ models (trained using the 160GB corpus) with T5 (trained using the 800GB C4 corpus)** .

Moreover, **in all our comparisons with T5, we include a T5 baseline trained by ourselves using exactly the same 160GB corpus and the same hyperparameters** . So the comparison between Metro-T5 and our T5 baseline is completely fair. Most claims regarding our method in our paper are based on this fair comparison.

Table 2 in the paper also includes the comparison between Metro-T5 and BART in the Base setting. We choose T5 as our main baseline because (a) the T5 paper includes experimental results on a greater variety of settings and tasks that we can reference; (b) the T5 has a better overall performance so it is a stronger baseline.

content.title: Response to Reviewer d7ab (Part 2)
content.comment:
### Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility Question 1

> Authors keep trying to relate the work to METRO, which is not as well known as BART/ELEKTRA/T5, and this does not seem necessary at all. The pre-training objective is very similar to BART, but instead the noise is provided by an ELECTRA-like auxiliary model. I would strongly recommend re-writing the paper to relate it to ELECTRA+BART instead of relating to METRO. The former are much better known to most readers and the relationship appears stronger as well.

Indeed, the final pretraining objective described in this paper shares similarities with ELECTRA and BART. However, we still call our method Metro-T5 because:

1. The proposed method is related to METRO because it integrates a binary replaced token detection (RTD) task with a corrective language modeling (CLM) task as METRO does. The decoder in Metro-T5 is doing corrections instead of masked language modeling as in BART. The proposed method is related to T5 because the finetuning pipeline is very similar to T5. In single-task finetuning for text classification, T5 and Metro-T5 decode the label as a sequence of text, without adding any new parameters to the model. However, BART feeds the whole input sequence into the decoder, takes the CLS token's output state as the representation, and initializes a new linear classifier to classify the output state.
1. One of our major empirical contributions is that Metro-T5 outperforms T0-3B in the T0-Eval prompting benchmark. Both the baseline (T0-3B) and the benchmark (T0-Eval) are from the work by Sanh et al. (2022), an influential work in the area of prompt learning, and this work is also based solely on T5. The studies of BART on prompting are less thorough compared with T0, thus we use the latter as the main baseline.


### Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility Question 2

> For Figure 4, does this pretraining time correspond to FLOPs? Is it possible to simply use FLOPs instead or as well?

Yes, the pretraining wall time in Figure 4 corresponds with FLOPs, because we are training both models using the same hardware/software environment. Reporting wall time is a standard practice followed by related works, including COCO-LM (Meng et al., 2021). We will make this more clear in the paper.

### Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility Question 3

> Reproducibility: There are significant missing details on how to train T5 and the auxiliary model "side-by-side". At least some pseudo-code would be helpful.
> e.g. How do you deal with sampling step (generating x^noise) from the auxiliary model? Do you take the argmax? Do you stop gradients for encoder-decoder flowing past x^noise? How do you set the lambda hparams in the loss?

To sample $x^\text{noise}$, Metro-T5 samples one token for each mask from the softmax distribution predicted by the auxiliary model. Following related works (Clark et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021), the gradient from the main model is not back-propagated to the auxiliary model via $x^\text{noise}$. We set lambda hyperparameters (1:50:1) following Meng et al. 2021 and never tuned these hyperparameters.

We added these details in Appendix A.2. Thank you for your helpful suggestions.

**References**

- Kevin Clark, Minh-Thang Luong, Quoc V Le, and Christopher D Manning. ELECTRA: Pre-training text encoders as discriminators rather than generators. In ICLR, 2020.
- Yu Meng, Chenyan Xiong, Payal Bajaj, Saurabh Tiwary, Paul Bennett, Jiawei Han, and Xia Song. COCO-LM: Correcting and contrasting text sequences for language model pretraining. In Proceedings of NeurIPS 2021, 2021.
- Hangbo Bao, Li Dong, Furu Wei, Wenhui Wang, Nan Yang, Xiaodong Liu, Yu Wang, Songhao Piao, Jianfeng Gao, Ming Zhou, and Hsiao-Wuen Hon. UniLMv2: Pseudo-masked language models for unified language model pre-training. In ICML, 2020.
- Mike Lewis, Yinhan Liu, Naman Goyal, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Abdelrahman Mohamed, Omer Levy, Ves Stoyanov, and Luke Zettlemoyer. BART: Denoising sequence-to-sequence pre-training for natural language generation, translation, and comprehension. In ACL, 2019.
- Yinhan Liu, Myle Ott, Naman Goyal, Jingfei Du, Mandar Joshi, Danqi Chen, Omer Levy, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Veselin Stoyanov. RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach. arXiv, 1907.11692.
- Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, and Peter J Liu. Exploring the limits of transfer learning with a unified text-to-text transformer. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2019.
- Victor Sanh, Albert Webson, Colin Raffel, Stephen Bach, Lintang Sutawika, Zaid Alyafeai, Antoine Chaffin, Arnaud Stiegler, Arun Raja, Manan Dey, M Saiful Bari, Canwen Xu, Urmish Thakker, Shanya Sharma Sharma, Eliza Szczechla, Taewoon Kim, Gunjan Chhablani, Nihal Nayak, et al. Multitask Prompted Training Enables Zero-Shot Task Generalization. In ICLR, 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed to combine T5 with ELECTRA style training objectives (i.e., detect replaced tokens). The main argument for this combination is that pretrained models are either good for NLU (encoder only) or NLG (decoder-only/encoder-decoder). The paper proposed a method called Metro-T5, which trains the encoder in T5 with RTD objective and the decoder with standard conditional LM objective.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

The author reimplemented T5 and compared Metro-T5 vs T5 in base size settings. The results show a nice improvement of Metro-T5 over T5 in fine-tuning setup. Metro-T5 also works better than T5 in zero-shot prompt based setup.

### Weaknesses
- The proposed metro-T5 is incremental
- On NLU tasks (Table 2) Metro-T5 is on par with previous pre-training model COCO-LM
- Comparing Metro-T5 with T0-XL is misleading. It is nice to see the improvement over T0-XL (with 3B params) on T0-validation sets, but it is worth pointing out that (1). T0-XL wasn’t meant to set the best performance. T0 paper simply asks the question “Can zero-shot generalization instead be directly induced by explicit multitask learning?” and it answered that. (2) From technical perspective, T0 paper noted the problem that T5 wasn’t trained on proper target sequence and T0 is initialized from T5-adaptLM (Lester et al., 2021) which is more suitable for prompt. Metro-T5 is trained on full target sequence (i.e., Decode entire origin) which is better by design for prompt. Training the encoder is in Metro-T5 is also useful for NLU tasks (i.e., NLI and Coref) in table 3.  Having that said, I think “outperforming T0XL on T0 with only 8% of its parameters” doesn’t mean much.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is quite clear, easy to understand and follow. The novelty aspect is limited (based on the T5 and Electra combination). It should be easy to reproduce the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the proposed approach Metro-T5 seems marginal, the improvements of pretrained model Metro-T5 in full finetune and prompt based learning are not that impressive.

content.title: Response to Reviewer BVKi
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. Thank you for pointing out that “the results show a nice improvement of Metro-T5 over T5 in fine-tuning setup and zero-shot prompt based setup”. We present new results of larger models in the “general response” post. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> The proposed metro-T5 is incremental

Metro-T5 is the first model that uses model-generated signals in pretraining encoder-decoder models. We resolve various challenges in the design of pretraining objectives, and the resulting pretraining paradigm is significantly different from all previous works. The pretrained Metro-T5 is a unified model that has strong performance in NLU and NLG and achieves SOTA performance on prompt finetuning.

We have present a large amount of empirical studies in this paper. We conduct experiments on NLU (GLUE), NLG (QA, summarization), and prompt finetuning (T0-Eval). In all tasks, Metro-T5 is either on par or outperforms the T5 baseline with a comparable size. Moreover, Metro-T5-Base++ outperforms the T0-3B model on the T0-Eval benchmark with only 8% of its parameters.

### Weakness 2

> On NLU tasks (Table 2) Metro-T5 is on par with previous pre-training model COCO-LM

Metro-T5 is on par with Metro-LM on the GLUE NLU benchmark. However, Metro-LM is an encoder-only model that cannot do summarization and generative prompt finetuning. In contrast, **Metro-T5 is a unified model** that is not only the first non-encoder-only model that achieves such performance in NLU, but also can do NLG (text summarization) and prompt finetuning with SOTA performance.

### Weakness 3

> Comparing Metro-T5 with T0-XL is misleading. It is nice to see the improvement over T0-XL (with 3B params) on T0-validation sets, but it is worth pointing out that (1). T0-XL wasn’t meant to set the best performance. T0 paper simply asks the question “Can zero-shot generalization instead be directly induced by explicit multitask learning?” and it answered that. (2) From technical perspective, T0 paper noted the problem that T5 wasn’t trained on proper target sequence and T0 is initialized from T5-adaptLM (Lester et al., 2021) which is more suitable for prompt. Metro-T5 is trained on full target sequence (i.e., Decode entire origin) which is better by design for prompt. Training the encoder is in Metro-T5 is also useful for NLU tasks (i.e., NLI and Coref) in table 3. Having that said, I think “outperforming T0XL on T0 with only 8% of its parameters” doesn’t mean much.

We would argue that T0 authors have done a great job in pushing the performance of their T0 models. As reflected in later research (Wei et al., 2022), **T0 results are considered strong state-of-the-art baselines**. Many recent works leverage a much larger set of training tasks to outperform it (Wei et al., 2021).

We like to clarify that, according to Sanh et al. (2021), T0-3B (and T0-11B) is based on LM-adapted T5-3B (or T5-11B) and then finetuned on the T0 Train multitask mixture. Note that the LM-adaptation step is introduced to improve the prompt learning performance, which consumes more compute. The pipeline of T0 is:

```
[T5 pretraining] -> [LM adaptation] -> [T0 prompt finetuning].  
```

We are comparing against the strong T0 baseline **using the same finetuning pipeline** . The "Metro-T5" rows shown in Table 3 of our paper are trained using a similar pipeline. We finetune pretrained Metro-T5 on exactly the same T0 Train multitask mixture. So the pipeline is:

```
[Metro-T5 pretraining] -> [T0 prompt finetuning].
```

And then each finetuned model is evaluated on the T0 Eval multitask mixture. Table 3 shows that prompt-finetuned Metro-T5-Base++ outperforms T0-3B, so there is enough evidence to claim that *"Metro-T5-Base++ outperforms T5-3B"*.

As discussed in the general response, we train Metro-T5-Large++ (24L, 1024D, 775M parameters). The result is shown in the table in the “general response” post. As is shown in the table, Metro-T5-Large++ outperforms Metro-T5-Base++ and T0-3B and is only 1.8 pts below T0-11B with only 7% of its parameters.

**References**

- Jason Wei, Maarten Bosma, Vincent Y. Zhao, Kelvin Guu, Adams Wei Yu, Brian Lester, Nan Du, Andrew M. Dai, Quoc V. Le. Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners. arXiv, 2109.01652.
- Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, Maarten Bosma, Brian Ichter, Fei Xia, Ed Chi, Quoc Le, Denny Zhou. Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models. arXiv, 2201.11903.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper improves encoder-decoder pre-training models such as T5 with ELECTRA-style model-generated signals. The authors analyze the challenges of pre-training T5 with model-generated signals. Then, they devise Metro-T5 including a new denoising pre-training task and a multi-task training objective combined with ELECTRA. Experimental results show that Metro-T5 outperforms T5 on a variety of language tasks in standard fine-tuning and prompt-based zero/few-shot scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1) The experimental results are relatively strong. In addition to fully supervised settings, the authors also show the improvement in the few-shot / zero-shot setting with prompt tuning / instruction tuning, which provides some insights on the relationship between the ability of few-shot learning and the design of pre-training tasks.

2) This paper is overall well-written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

1) The proposed method which incorporates ELECTRA into T5 lacks intuition and motivation. First, in Section 1, the authors say that “recent research raises concerns on whether such unified models come with inferior downstream effectiveness and scaling efficiency”. However, the reasons for inferior performance of encoder-decoder pre-trained models are not clearly described. Then, the authors say that they choose to introduce ELECTRA because “pre-training with model-generated signals provides strong efficiency and effectiveness benefits on encoder models”. I wonder whether there is a specific research problem of T5 that can be directly solved by ELECTRA-style pre-training. Also, as we are in 2022, there are already some works that outperform ELECTRA in pre-training encoder-only models. Thus, the reason to incorporate ELECTRA should be further clarified.

2) From Figure 2, Metro-T5 seems incremental compared with existing works. This pre-training fashion including a bidirectional encoder which predicts masked information based on corrupted inputs and a unidirectional decoder which acts as a causal language model has already been explored in existing works like PEGASUS [1] (although I understand that they are slightly different in encoder input corruption and encoder pre-training tasks).

3) In Section 5.3 and Figure 3b, the training instability is not intuitively presented because Figure 3b doesn’t give the variance among different runs. From this figure, I can only see the performance gap among different pre-training tasks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer xYAR (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. According to your comments, we updated the paper and added missing references and comparisons. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> The proposed method which incorporates ELECTRA into T5 lacks intuition and motivation. First, in Section 1, the authors say that “recent research raises concerns on whether such unified models come with inferior downstream effectiveness and scaling efficiency”. However, the reasons for inferior performance of encoder-decoder pre-trained models are not clearly described. Then, the authors say that they choose to introduce ELECTRA because “pre-training with model-generated signals provides strong efficiency and effectiveness benefits on encoder models”. I wonder whether there is a specific research problem of T5 that can be directly solved by ELECTRA-style pre-training. Also, as we are in 2022, there are already some works that outperform ELECTRA in pre-training encoder-only models. Thus, the reason to incorporate ELECTRA should be further clarified.

Metro-T5 is indeed motivated by related works about pretraining Transformer encoders (BERT) using model-generated signals, such as ELECTRA, COCO-LM, and METRO-LM. However, encoder-decoder models like T5 support NLG and prompting, but they underperform state-of-the-art encoder-only models on NLU. Our motivation is to bring in one of the most beneficial techniques, model-generated training signals, from encoder-only models to T5. The goal is to provide one unified pretrained model that excels on a wide variety of tasks, namely, NLU, NLG, and prompt-based learning, which help reduce the duplicated computing cost in pretraining several models dedicated to different scenarios.

In both BERT and T5, the input sentence or sentence pair is fed into the pretrained encoder. The only difference is that BERT uses a simple linear classifier for label prediction, while T5 uses the pretrained decoder to generate labels as a target sequence. Therefore, the **motivation is very clear that methods used to improve BERT pretraining can also help T5 to learn better, at least on NLU tasks** .

Based on this motivation, the technical contribution of this paper mainly focuses on the objective designs for improving training stability and improving the effectiveness of encoder-decoder models on a large set of target scenarios. The empirical gain of Metro-T5 is significant: it outperforms the T5 baseline significantly on NLU, elevating encoder-decoder to the same effectiveness as encoder-only models, at the same time it also achieves state-of-the-art results on NLG and prompt finetuning.

We denote *“ELECTRA-style models”* as LMs pretrained with model-generated signals to attribute the credit to ELECTRA which is the origin of this idea. The exact technique that we are incorporating into T5 is METRO-LM (Bajaj et al., 2022). METRO-LM is now the state-of-the-art pretrained encoder-only model (as is reflected by the GLUE leaderboard) until the date of this submission.

### Weakness 2

> From Figure 2, Metro-T5 seems incremental compared with existing works. This pre-training fashion including a bidirectional encoder which predicts masked information based on corrupted inputs and a unidirectional decoder which acts as a causal language model has already been explored in existing works like PEGASUS [1] (although I understand that they are slightly different in encoder input corruption and encoder pre-training tasks).

We updated our paper, and the new version cites PEGASUS and compares METRO-T5 and PEGASUS on the task of summarization.

- Metro-T5 and PEGASUS are different on many fronts. Here are some notable differences.
PEGASUS proposes a novel **gap sentence generation (GSG)** pretraining objective, which is a *rule-based* objective that focuses on text summarization. In contrast, METRO-T5's pretraining signal comes from an auxiliary model, so the pretraining objective is *model-based*.

- METRO-T5 has a strong performance not only in language generation but also in text classification and prompting. PEGASUS mainly focuses on language generation, especially text summarization.

content.title: Response to Reviewer xYAR (Part 2)
content.comment:
### Weakness 3

> In Section 5.3 and Figure 3b, the training instability is not intuitively presented because Figure 3b doesn’t give the variance among different runs. From this figure, I can only see the performance gap among different pre-training tasks.

The instability in optimization can result in two consequences. The first is **high variance in the optimization result** , which is what you refer to and is often studied by showing the variances of the model with multiple runs. The second one is when the instability breaks the optimization process, resulting in **diverged training runs** . This is more severe and is a significant challenge in model pretraining. For example, when training OPT (Zhang et al., 2022) and BLOOM (Scao et al., 2022), researchers have to overcome a ton of diverged training runs due to training instability to even have one successfully trained model. **The instability we are facing in this work is the second category** . As shown in Figure 3b, without proper techniques, the pretraining is prone to divergence.

content.title: General Response to all Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their helpful comments. We uploaded a revision of the paper. Here is a list of changes:

- Cite PEGASUS (Zheng et al., 2020) and add comparisons between Metro-T5 and PEGASUS into Table 2 on text summarization. (reviewer xYAR, weakness 2)

- Add details of the sampling method used to sample training signals and how we choose loss weight ($\lambda$) hyperparameters into Appendix A.2. (reviewer d7ab, reproducibility concerns)

- Add a new appendix section, Appendix A.5, explaining the challenge of ill-formed target (Section 3.2) leading to ambiguities by a concrete example. (reviewer R8zZ, weakness 1)

Multiple reviewers (BVKi, d7ab, R8zZ) ask for **experimental results on large-scale setups** . Here, we present the result of Metro-T5-Large++ on T0 setting. The *Large++* model has 24 layers on the encoder and 24 layers on the decoder, each has a hidden dimension of 1,024, comparable to T5-Large. Metro-T5-Large++ has 775M parameters. The model is trained on the 160GB corpus with 512 tokens per sequence and 2,048 tokens per batch, the same as *Base++*, but trained 1.2M steps (rather than 2M steps).
